Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed with Mahmudual Islam and Nihad Kabir, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners. 
Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan Addl, AG with Kaiseruddin Ahmed DAG, Mashuque Hossain Ahmed AAG, Saidur Rahman AAG and Md. Sirajul Hoque AAG ----- For the Respondent No.1
parties:
Bangladesh Retired Government Employees Welfare Association, represented by its President Kafiluddin Mahmood and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary to the Ministry of Finance, Finance Division, Government of Bangladesh and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment: 3. According to the averment in the writ petition, the petitioner No. 2 joined the erstwhile Civil Service of Pakistan on 16.10.1950., After liberation of Bangladesh he served the Government of Bangladesh and retired on 3.3.1983 from the post of Secretary, Ministry of Finance, Government of Bangladesh. The petitioner No. 2 was appointed to the erstwhile Police Service of Pakistan on 7.1.1952 and after liberation of Bangladesh he served the Government of Bangladesh and retired on 1.8.83 from the post of Secretary to the Ministry of Defence. It is emphasised that since British Rule in India the Government employees are being paid superannuation pension by the government and this pension to the retired employees is not a bounty paid by the State but is an essential term and condition of their service and is paid on consideration of the obligation of the State not to leave its employees who rendered service in the useful span of life to penury in their old age and disability and infirmity of their body and mind. According to the petitioners, apart from a statutory obligation of the State the superannuation pension is aimed at providing the retired government employees a life free from want, of decency and self-respect, and according to the standard equivalent to their pre-retirement level. Moreover, the pension paid to retired government employees is governed by Civil Service Regulations and various other Rules. It is also stated that initially the system of pension was introduced by the then government of India under British Rule in the year 1924 and, subsequently, the Rules relating to pension underwent various changes and the rates of pension were thereby modified. In short, prior to 1.7.66 the rate of pension was 50% of average pay of a government employee calculated on the basis of a certain table on completion of 25 years of service or more. With effect from 1.7.66 the rate of pension was revised under Notification No. F/IU-12/66/93 dated 2.9.66 and by this the rate of pension was fixed at 50% of average pay on completion of 25 years of service and 60% of average pay on completion of 30 years of service and the maximum ceiling was fixed at Taka 1000.00 per month. With effect from 1.7.74 by issuing Notification No. MF(IC)-11-14/74 dated 21.1.74 the rate of pension was fixed at 60% of the last pay drawn on completion of 25 years of service. With effect from 1.7.77 the scale of pension was again revised by Notification No. MF(ID)-1-2/77/856 dated 20.12.77 whereby the maximum ceiling of pension was raised to Taka 1500.00 per month. With effect from 1.7.82 the rate of pension was again revised by issuing Notification No. MFP (FD) Regn-1/3P-22/82-147 dated 21.12.82 and MFP (FD) Regn-1/3P-22/82-117 dated 1.8.83 and by these notifications the rate of pension was fixed at 60% of the last pay on completion of 25 years of service and the minimum pension was fixed at Taka 100.00 per month and the maximum ceiling was raised to Taka 1800.00 per month. With effect from 1.6.85 the rate of pension was again revised and fixed at 70% of the last pay on completion of 25 years of service the maximum ceiling being fixed at Taka 4000.00 per month by issuing Notification No. MF (Regn- 1) 3P-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85. The last revision of the rate of pension took place with effect from 1.7.89 under Notification Nos. অম (বিধি)-১/৩ পি-২৮/৮৫/১০৬ dated 4.11.89 and অম (বিধি)-১/৩ পি-২৮/৮৫/৬১ dated 5.7.89 whereby the rate of pension was raised to 80% of average pay on completion of 25 years of service and the maximum ceiling was fixed at Taka 5000.00 per month. On 1.7.91 by Notification No. অম/অবি (প্রবিধি)-৩ পি- ২৮/৮৫/৫০(১০০০) dated 4.12.91 the maximum ceiling was fixed at Taka 8200.00 per month. In this connection, it should be added that upto 1.7.74 i.e coming into force of the rate of pension vide Notification No. MF(IC)-11-14/74 dated 21st January, 1974 calculation of average emoluments was specified and by this notification it was provided that the pension table should be made on the basis of emoluments which the government employee was receiving immediately before his retirement i.e. the last pay drawn by the government employee on the date of his retirement. The same principle has been followed in the latest Notification i.e. Memo No. ME (Regn-1)3P-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85 as at Annexure-C to the writ petition which is impugned in this case. In addition to pension certain other benefits such as, commutation of pension and payment of lumpsum-amount in lieu thereof known as gratuity and of net payment of a lump-sum amount of 12 months salary last drawn by the government employees were also allowed to government employees on retirement. But these need not detain us here as these are not the subject-matter of controversy in this writ petition. It is next alleged by the petitioners that after liberation of Bangladesh there has been high inflation and the purchasing power of taka gradually eroded as a result of which the government of Bangladesh had to revise the pay scales of government employees in 1973, 1977 and 1985. As an example, it has been stated that in 1973 the pay of a Secretary to the Government was fixed at Taka 3000.00 per month and then ultimately the pay of the Secretary was raised to Taka 6000.00 per month in 1985. Similarly, the pay scale of the Deputy Secretary in 1973 was 850-1650 with certain special pay and this pay scale was revised and raised to Taka 1850-2075 and then ultimately to Taka 3700-4825 in the year 1985. As we have already observed, previous to 1974 the pension was to be calculated on the basis of emoluments drawn by a government employee during the 12 months preceding the date of his retirement. But with effect from 1.7.74 this was done away with and pension was to be calculated on the basis of the last pay drawn by each employee. According to the petitioners, by the pension rules brought into effect vide Memo No. MF(Regn-1)3P-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85 as at Annexure-C, substantial difference in the pension benefit between the pensioners who had retired before 1.6.85 and those who retired on or after 1.6.85, was made. As an example, it has been stated that a Secretary to the Government who was drawing a salary of Taka 3000.00 per month retiring before 1.6.84 and between 1.6.84 and 31.5.85 is to draw a pension of Taka 900.00 per month, whereas a Secretary retiring on or after 1.6.85 was allowed to draw a net pension of Taka 2000.00 per month. Similarly, an employee retiring from the lowest scale of salary of Taka 225-315 was granted a pension of Taka 94.5 per month if retired prior to 1.6.84 and between 1.6.84 and 31.5.85, and Taka 258.00 per month if retired on or after 1.6.85. This obviously took place because of the revision of the scales of pay and enhancement of pay of all government employees before coming into force of the impugned pension rules on 1.6.85. The petitioners claim that all retired government employees receiving pension are pensioners forming a homogeneous class and, as such, payment of different scales of pension to the pensioners retiring from the service on the basis of the date of retirement is an irrational classification, violative of the equality clause enshrined in Article 27 of the Constitution and, as such, cannot, be sustained and must be knocked down as unconstitutional. According to the petitioners, irrespective of the rise in pay scale of the government employees from time to time against which they have no grievance, all government employees retiring from a particular post being pensioners are entitled to receive pension on the basis of the existing ply of the said post. In short, they claim pension on "presumptive pay" irrespective of the dates of retirement. Although in this writ petition, ultimately the petitioners have mainly claimed computation of pension of all pensioners retiring prior to 1.6.85 on the basis of the pay of the post existing on that date or equivalent post if that post ceases to exist i.e. on "presumptive pay" these is another aspect in this case i.e. the constitutionality of the pension table introduced by Notification No. MF(Regn-1) 3P-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85 as at Annexure-C whereby the rate of pension was raised to 70% of the emoluments and also Notification No. অম (বিধি-১) ৩ পি-২৮/৮৫/১০৬ dated 4.11.89 whereby the table was again revised and the rate of pension was raised to 80% of the emoluments or last pay drawn on completion of 25 years' service. Along with this the rate of pension was also raised according to the length of service of each employee the minimum qualifying service being 10 years and the maximum being 25 years. According to the petitioners, the payment of different rates of pension to the pensioners retiring from the cadre post prior to 1.6.85 from those retiring from the same post on or after 1.6.85 has been absolutely arbitrary being contrary to the principle of classification and, therefore, violative of the equality clause as enshrined in Article 27 of the Constitution.
